hook: I lent money to a friend and they **won't pay it back.**
hook_q: Is not returning borrowed money a crime?

slides.title: Usually, it's a **civil** matter.
slides.body: The Supreme Court has said that mere breach of contract cannot lead to a criminal case for cheating, unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right from the beginning.
slides.ref: Supreme Court · Delhi Race Club, 2024 INSC 626

slides.title: Cheating needs a **false promise.**
slides.body: A promise becomes a deception only if it was made without any intention of keeping it. A dishonest intention can't be presumed just because the promise wasn't kept.

slides.title: Your remedy: a **civil suit.**
slides.body: You can file a civil suit to recover the amount. The Supreme Court has said the criminal process is not a tool to force someone to pay.

timeline.text: For a suit for money lent, the **limitation** clock usually starts when the loan is made.
The period to file. A suit filed after the prescribed period **shall be dismissed.**

slides.title: Signed note or part-payment? **Fresh period.**
slides.body: If, before time runs out, the borrower signs a written acknowledgment of the debt, or makes a payment towards it (acknowledged in writing), a fresh limitation period starts from then.

sources: Supreme Court: Delhi Race Club (1940) Ltd. v. State of U.P., 2024 INSC 626 (sci.gov.in)
Supreme Court: Parag Kishore Satoskar v. State of Jharkhand, 2026 INSC 846 (sci.gov.in)
caption:
Lent money and not getting it back? Here's what the law says. 👇

1️⃣ Not repaying is usually a civil matter, not cheating
2️⃣ It can be cheating only if there was a fraudulent or dishonest intention right from the beginning
3️⃣ Your remedy is a civil suit to recover the money. The criminal process can't be used just to force payment
4️⃣ For a suit for money lent, you usually get 3 years from when the loan is made
5️⃣ A signed acknowledgment or a part-payment (acknowledged in writing) before time runs out starts a fresh period

Source: Supreme Court (2024 INSC 626; 2026 INSC 846); Limitation Act, 1963 (Sec 3, 18, 19; Schedule Art 19, 21)
